question: The background picture in Oil Ocean fills the console's background picture memory completely, right up to a hardware wall, so the parallax editor cannot add a single new moving band to it. Not even the smallest one. The wall is real and cannot be moved: the background tiles end exactly where the sprite table begins, and every last slot is holding a distinct piece of artwork with no duplicates, no blank tiles and no mirrored pairs left to reclaim. The tool that drew the current background was never told to leave any room, so it used all of it. The version of that tool used before it deliberately kept about a hundred slots back for animation, and that reservation is what got lost. Whether the background art gets redrawn to make room is an art call, and it is yours.

options.what: Parts of the background that are already drawn can be turned into moving bands. This works on the real level today and needs no picture memory at all, because nothing new is drawn. What you cannot do is add a new moving element, or move artwork somewhere it is not already sitting. The four empty band slots stay empty.
options.costs: No art work and no waiting. One check is still outstanding on my side: the end to end path has been proven with a band built by the code, not yet with one built by hand in the editor. That check is a queue item and about an hour.

options.name: Redraw the background with room kept back for animation
options.what: The art tool gets told to stop short of the wall and keep slots free. Every band slot then becomes usable for anything you want to put in it, and the two animated bands that the last art run wiped out can come back at the same time.
options.costs: The background picture loses roughly a quarter of its distinct detail, which is a thing you would see if you stopped and looked at the sky and the rig. It costs one art run plus your eyes on the result, and it is work on the engine side rather than mine.

recommend.because: It puts a moving background on screen without touching art you already approved, and it is the only one of the two that can start today. If you later decide to redraw and keep room back, adding bands from scratch starts working on its own and none of the work built so far is wasted. So this is not a road that has to be undone, it is the first half of the same road.

question: When you fix a chunk in the library, should every place you already stamped it fix itself too? Right now, in the aeon half of the editor, no — a stamp copies the tiles in and forgets where they came from, so correcting a chunk means finding and re-stamping every copy by hand. The odd part is that the CLASSIC half of the same editor already works the other way, on purpose. This surfaced because an agent asked to read a region's chunk ids back and there are none to read.

options.what: Leave it. A stamp stays a one-time copy, and fixing a chunk means re-stamping its copies yourself.
options.costs: Every correction to a piece of scenery is manual and easy to miss one. It also means an agent can never answer 'what is this region made of' — it can only see loose tiles. Costs you nothing today and gets more expensive the more level you build.

options.what: Make aeon sections remember the chunk, like the classic half already does. Edit a chunk once and every placement updates.
options.costs: A real change to how a level is stored, touching stamping, copy-paste, save/load and export, and it needs a decision about what happens to a placement you have since painted over by hand. Medium-sized, and it is the kind of change that is much cheaper now than after you have built more level.

options.what: Record the chunk a stamp came from as provenance only — the editor can tell you 'this came from chunk 12', but editing the chunk does not change it.
options.costs: Much smaller, and it unlocks the agent-readable answer and a 'find every copy of this' command. But it does NOT give you the propagate-on-edit behaviour, and a label that looks like a link but is not is its own kind of trap.

recommend: Make aeon sections remember the chunk (option 2)
because: Your own editor already made this call once and made it the other way: the classic document is explicitly a 'never flatten' model — tiles, blocks, chunks, chunk-id layout — written that way so shared-chunk edits propagate exactly as the game's own data does, because a Mega Drive level IS a grid of chunk ids. The aeon half flattens instead, so the same tool answers the same question two opposite ways depending on which project you opened. That is worth resolving on purpose rather than by accident, and the cost only grows with the amount of level you have drawn. I am not asking you to schedule it now — I am asking whether the flattening is a decision or an oversight, because everything downstream (the agent read, propagate-on-edit, 'find every copy') is gated behind the answer.

question: You answered d-18 with a shape none of my three options had — in your words: "what if by default it does one way and we have a checkbox that allows the other?" That settles the SHAPE: both behaviours exist, one is the default, the other is a checkbox. It leaves exactly one thing open, and it is the part that decides whether a wrong guess is recoverable: WHICH ONE IS THE DEFAULT?

options.what: DEFAULT = the stamp remembers its chunk (edits propagate); the checkbox is "detach this copy", which turns one placement into loose tiles that stop tracking.
options.costs: The bigger build: stamping, copy-paste, save/load and export all have to carry the chunk id. Detaching must also work on a placement you already painted over by hand, or the escape hatch is missing where you most need it.

options.what: DEFAULT = the stamp flattens as it does today; the checkbox is "keep this linked to the chunk", which opts a placement into propagation.
options.costs: Cheaper to build and it changes nothing about level files you already have. But every stamp you place without ticking the box destroys the chunk id at that moment, so those placements can never be linked afterwards and an agent still cannot answer 'what is this region made of' for most of the level.

recommend: DEFAULT = the stamp remembers its chunk; the checkbox detaches.
because: One asymmetry decides it and it is not a matter of taste: the two defaults are not equally recoverable. Detaching later is ALWAYS possible — the tiles are right there, and turning a link into a copy needs no information you do not already have. Linking later is NOT possible, because flattening throws the chunk id away at the moment of the stamp, and nothing afterwards can tell whether a patch of tiles came from chunk 12 or was drawn by hand to look like it. So default-remember can be undone per placement whenever you change your mind; default-flatten quietly makes an irreversible choice on every stamp you place before you have decided. It also matches the half of your own editor that already made this call: the classic document is explicitly a never-flatten model because a Mega Drive level IS a grid of chunk ids. ONE SUB-QUESTION I am folding in rather than filing separately, tell me if you disagree: I read your checkbox as available BOTH at stamp time and afterwards on an existing placement, because 'a placement you have since painted over by hand' was the open cost in the original option 2 and an after-the-fact detach is exactly what answers it.

question: After you click Clear or Reset in the collision palette, that button keeps keyboard focus - and pressing SPACE fires the whole wipe again, with no confirmation. Enter does not. Both wipes are one Ctrl+Z away and the undo restores everything, so nothing is lost permanently; the question is whether an idle Space should be able to wipe a plane at all. Space activating a focused button is standard platform behaviour, so changing it trades a small surprise for a small inconsistency.

options.what: The button gives up focus after it fires, so a later Space does nothing. Clicking it again still works normally.
options.costs: A keyboard-only author loses the ability to repeat the action with Space; they would tab back to it. Smallest change, no dialog.

options.what: A confirmation when the wipe would destroy bits you do not own - which is the only case that can lose work you cannot re-derive.
options.costs: A dialog in the middle of a fast operation. Both buttons already toast what they did, so this adds friction to a recoverable action.

options.what: Nothing changes. It is one undo away and Space-activates-focused-button is what every other button in the app does.
options.costs: An idle keypress can wipe a plane. You would find out by seeing the toast, and the fix is Ctrl+Z.

recommend.because: It removes the surprise without adding a dialog to an action that is already fully recoverable and already announces itself with a toast. The other two either interrupt a fast operation or leave a wholesale wipe on an idle keystroke. THIS IS A FEEL CALL AND IT IS YOURS - I have not changed anything. Measured, not assumed: the wipe was fired by Space with the button still focused, and proven exactly as recoverable as the clicked one. Enter does not fire it, which is why this reads as an accident rather than a design.

question: 82 of our test harnesses open the aeon or s1disasm folder directly - the real one you and the other agents are editing, not a copy. Two that could also WRITE to it are now fixed and a third is being fixed. The question is what to do about the other 79, which only READ. Do we require every harness to work on its own copy, or is reading the real folder acceptable when the harness proves it changed nothing?

options.what: COPY ALWAYS. Every harness refuses to run against the real folder; each one makes its own copy first.
options.costs: Roughly a day of agent time across 79 files, and every one of those harnesses gets slower to run (a copy of aeon per run). In exchange, no test can ever be coloured by what another agent has half-typed in their folder, and no test can ever write into one.

options.what: COPY ONLY WHERE IT CAN WRITE. Harnesses that merely read keep using the real folder; only ones that open an editable project or save get the copy.
options.costs: Cheap - the write-capable ones are the three already handled. But a reading harness still has its result decided by whoever is mid-edit next door: that is exactly how a green test that meant nothing went unnoticed for its whole life here, and how one went red last week with a stack trace naming no repo, which three agents filed as unrelated.

options.what: LEAVE IT AND WRITE IT DOWN. Fix nothing further; record the 82 files as known, with the reasoning.
options.costs: Free today. The cost is that the next agent to hit a mystery red spends the afternoon three of them already spent, and we keep a class of test whose pass and fail are both decided outside this repo.

recommend: COPY ONLY WHERE IT CAN WRITE

question: The sprite size chips and the New button replace the whole sprite document, and they also THROW AWAY the undo history - so unlike the collision Clear/Reset you just ruled on, that one is not one Ctrl+Z away. Worse, the replacement marks the new blank document as having no unsaved edits, so the dirty dot goes out and the guards that normally stop you losing work on tab-close or project-open have nothing left to fire on. One misclick on a size chip and the sprite is gone with no undo, no warning, and nothing downstream that will ask. Separately from this, those buttons are being made to drop focus like the collision ones, so a stray keypress can no longer reach them; this card is only about a deliberate click.

options.what: If the sprite has unsaved edits, it asks before replacing it. A clean document gets no dialog at all - you only ever see it in the case where something would actually be lost.
options.costs: A confirmation on a path that is usually a deliberate start-over. Someone spinning up several new sprites in a row from a dirty one sees it each time.

options.what: Starting a new sprite becomes undoable - Ctrl+Z brings the old document back, the way it does everywhere else in the editor.
options.costs: The undo stack then walks backwards across two unrelated documents, which is a strange thing to step through. It also fights an invariant the code states on purpose - a fresh sprite is supposed to start with an empty history - so this is the largest of the three changes.

options.what: Nothing changes beyond the focus fix already going in. A button labelled New that makes a new sprite is doing what it says.
options.costs: A misclick on a size chip - which sits in the option bar beside tools you use constantly - discards the sprite with no undo and no warning, and clears the flag that would otherwise make the app ask you later.

recommend.because: It is the only one of the three where the cost is paid ONLY in the case that can lose work: a clean document never sees a dialog. The machinery already exists and is already used for exactly this question - tab close and project open both route through the same confirm store - so this is consistency rather than a new pattern. keep_undo is the bigger change and argues with an invariant the code states deliberately, and leave_it accepts an unrecoverable loss on a misclick, which is what separated these chips from the collision buttons in the first place: those were always one undo away, and this is not. MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED: newSprite calls activeSpriteHistory().clear() at spriteStore.ts:637 and replaces the document with blankDoc, which sets unsavedEdits false at :277. I have changed nothing about what these buttons do.

question: The Clear button in the Chunks section empties the whole chunk library, and Ctrl+Z does NOT bring it back. Measured on a real click: 71 chunks to 0, still 0 after undo, and the only thing that restored them was re-opening the project from disk. There is no confirmation. This is not the focus problem you ruled on in d-27 - that button does give up focus, because it removes itself from the screen when the library empties. It is a different and simpler problem: the one destructive control in this area that a single misclick cannot be taken back from.

options.what: It asks before clearing, the way closing a tab with unsaved work already does. Nothing else changes.
options.costs: A dialog on a button that some people press deliberately and often. It is the smallest change and the only one that stops the loss at the moment it would happen.

options.what: Clearing becomes a normal undoable action, so Ctrl+Z restores the library like it restores everything else.
options.costs: Chunk library changes deliberately sit OUTSIDE the undo history today - importing chunks is not undoable either. So this makes undo work for the clear but not for the import, which is its own kind of confusing, and it means the undo stack now holds a copy of the whole library.

options.what: Nothing changes. Re-opening the project brings the library back.
options.costs: A misclick silently empties the library with no warning and no undo, and the recovery is a step nobody would guess from the app - you have to know to re-open the project.
